completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidateRows: Fine-tuning strongly confirms theism over single-universe naturalism because life-permitting parameters are extremely improbable on naturalism but comparatively unsurprising if a perfectly good God values conscious moral life.
This is the pro side's principal likelihood argument and directly supplies the claimed evidential route from cosmic fine-tuning to theism.
After the introductory handoff, Miles defines the data and competing hypotheses, explains likelihood-based confirmation, and applies that framework to fine-tuning.

The stalking-horse objection fails because it would eliminate every possible empirical argument for God and because classical theism has greater intrinsic prior probability than contrived fine-tuning-specific naturalistic hypotheses.
These two defenses address the principal naturalistic challenge anticipated for the debate and preserve the comparative force of the fine-tuning inference.
Having completed his positive likelihood case, Miles introduces the anticipated augmented-naturalism objection and states a reductio response plus a prior-probability response.

Apparently artificial patterns can lose their intentional explanation after deeper scientific investigation, while even an unmistakably structured signal may support only generic intentionality rather than benevolent agency.
The examples establish the skeptical framework that unexpected structure need not warrant the richly specified personal explanation required by theism.
Miles's claim that fine-tuning is much likelier under a perfectly good divine creator than under naturalism.
Alex first recounts how pulsars displaced an alien hypothesis, then imagines a prime-number-framed transmission whose content supports an intentional source without revealing its character.

A message expressly claiming peaceful intent gives stronger evidence for intelligence than for benevolence, and similarly spectacular apparent biblical design would not securely identify a good God rather than a deceptive agent.
This analogy directly challenges the divine-psychology step needed to move from apparent purposive arrangement to the specific good-God hypothesis defended by the pro side.
Miles's inference from life-permitting order and valuable conscious life to the intentions of a perfectly good God.
Alex escalates his signal example to an English declaration of peace, highlights possible deception, and applies that gap between intentionality and goodness to apparent biblical signs.

Advanced aliens, future time travelers, or simulators could produce spectacular theistic-looking evidence, and the combined probability of such naturalistic alternatives should be compared with theism as a disjunction.
This is the con side's core hypothesis-space argument: theism must outperform the collective naturalistic alternative set, not merely one austere naturalistic hypothesis.
Miles's contention that contrived naturalistic alternatives cannot neutralize evidence favoring theism.
At the end of his opening, Alex supplies alien, time-travel, and simulation explanations, then argues that their probabilities belong in one disjunctive naturalistic comparison class.

If a fine-tuning-specific natural disposition can always be introduced to match the evidence, the same maneuver defeats every possible empirical case for theism, which is an implausibly sweeping consequence.
The argument is Miles's direct reply to the con opening and seeks to show that its hypothesis-augmentation method is globally self-defeating rather than locally successful.
Alex's use of tailored naturalistic hypotheses to explain even highly intentional-looking observations without theism.
Open discussion begins with Miles restating the proves-too-much objection, considering apparent messages in the stars, conceding reservations about that example, and pressing the general issue.

Bare comparisons between theism and naturalism are too vague or trivial; a powerful fine-tuning argument must specify a version of theism and show it explains the evidence better than every admissible version of naturalism.
This sets the con side's central burden-of-proof challenge by insisting that the relevant rival is the full naturalistic hypothesis space rather than a selectively weak member.
Miles's general claim that some empirical observations can rationally increase theism over naturalism.

Alex characterizes naturalism and theism as broad families, explains why pairwise comparisons between selected versions are uninteresting, and formulates the stronger universal comparison he would contest.
The intended claim compares classical theism with every hypothesis consistent with a defined single-universe naturalism, where the causal natural order exhausts reality relevant to the argument.
This clarification accepts the stronger comparative burden and fixes the hypothesis definitions on which the remainder of the fine-tuning dispute depends.
Alex's demand that the pro case specify its theism and outperform every version within the relevant naturalistic hypothesis class.
Miles narrows naturalism to a single-universe view of the natural world and identifies theism as an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly loving creator rather than a looser family.

Even a single-universe naturalism that excludes supernatural intervention retains expansive resources such as simulation, time travel, and advanced aliens, so it is unclear that any observation rules out all naturalistic explanations.
This applies the hypothesis-space objection to Miles's clarified naturalism and disputes the key claim that possible evidence could exhaust the naturalistic alternatives.
Miles's clarified assertion that classical theism can outperform every hypothesis permitted by his restricted definition of naturalism.
After discussion of causal naturalism and abstract objects, Alex accepts the framework provisionally but argues that it still permits many science-fiction-like causal explanations.

Directly witnessing Jesus emerge healed from his tomb, interact publicly for forty days, and ascend would provide at least some evidence for theism over naturalism despite alien, time-travel, or similar alternatives.
The example supplies a concrete countercase to the claim that naturalistic alternatives always prevent empirical observations from raising the probability of theism.
Alex's request for a concrete observation that supports theism after accounting for the many explanatory resources retained by naturalism.

Miles rejects the planets-forming-scripture example, substitutes an extended firsthand resurrection-and-ascension scenario, and argues that denying it all comparative force makes the objection implausibly universal.
An advanced alien civilization could produce the apparent resurrection signs, weakening their discriminatory force for theism.
The challenge directly tests whether striking empirical phenomena distinguish theism from naturalistic alternatives with unknown technological capacities.
Donahue's claim that witnessing Jesus's resurrection would provide strong evidence favoring theism over naturalism.
After Donahue presents a witnessed resurrection as an obvious counterexample to sweeping skepticism, Malpass proposes technologically advanced aliens as an alternative cause.
A resurrection fitting Jesus's life and claims is much less expected under a general alien hypothesis than under a religious interpretation.
It supplies the likelihood asymmetry needed for the resurrection example and challenges alternatives that could otherwise absorb every observation.
Malpass's suggestion that advanced aliens could produce all the observed features of an apparent resurrection.
Donahue accepts that alien causation is logically possible but argues that the event's historical and religious setting favors theism over a generic alien hypothesis.
General theism predicts a specific resurrection no better than general alienism, because both invoke powerful agents with largely unknown intentions.
The move attacks the alleged likelihood asymmetry by arguing that religious framing cannot establish which poorly understood agent caused the event.
Donahue's contention that Jesus's context makes resurrection more likely on theism than on a general alien hypothesis.
Malpass denies evasion, compares the predictive resources of a benevolent creator and aliens, and argues that apparent religious significance may itself be simulated.
Perfect goodness gives some grip on divine intentions, making revealed religion and resurrection more likely on theism than on generic alienism.
It identifies the divine attribute intended to generate a likelihood advantage and explains why tailoring an alien hypothesis merely relocates improbability.
Malpass's claim that divine and alien intentions are comparably unknowable and therefore lack an epistemic asymmetry.
Donahue argues that perfect goodness supports expectations of divine self-revelation, while increasingly specific alien alternatives pay an offsetting prior-probability cost.
A mildly specified alien motive can raise the likelihood of resurrection-like evidence without the severe prior penalty of an exact evidence-tailored hypothesis.
The move attempts to construct a naturalistic rival with enough intentional content to match theism while avoiding objectionable hyper-specificity.
Donahue's argument that alien explanations are technologically implausible or become prior-improbable when tailored to the evidence.
Malpass appeals to potentially immense technological advancement, accepts the penalty for exact tailoring, then proposes broad motives such as mischief or cultural influence.
Perfect-being theism occupies a substantial share of design possibilities, whereas life-directed augmented naturalism occupies a tiny share of naturalistic possibilities.
This is the core fine-tuning argument: the competing specifications receive sharply different conditional priors within their broader hypothesis spaces.
Malpass's attempt to create a modestly augmented alien or naturalistic hypothesis with predictive resources comparable to theism.
Donahue decomposes the hypotheses into general and specific forms, concedes simpler general naturalism, and argues that unlimited divine attributes make theism comparatively simple.
Naturalism includes broad simulation and science-fiction possibilities capable of accommodating nearly any observation, so evidence may never decisively separate it from theism.
The move articulates the hypothesis-space breadth underlying the skeptical position and its conclusion of persistent evidential underdetermination.
Donahue's division of design, perfect-being theism, and naturalism when comparing the sizes of their possibility spaces.
After clarifying that simulations belong on the naturalistic side, Malpass argues that naturalistic scenarios can explain almost anything that a theistic scenario could.
Simulation is independently skeptical and merely reproduces fine-tuning at base reality, while denying all possible empirical discrimination makes divine revelation impossible.
It answers a major naturalistic alternative both on its own merits and on explanatory regress, then presses a consequence of global ambiguity.
Malpass's claim that simulation hypotheses give naturalism broad resources to accommodate any apparently theistic evidence.
Donahue places simulation under naturalism, argues that ordinary anti-skeptical reasons count against it, and says a simulation would replicate fine-tuning in base reality.
Religious ambiguity and non-evidential faith are respectable Christian positions, so their acceptance cannot simply be treated as a reductio.
The move undercuts the pro side's principal intuitive objection by showing that empirical undecidability is a live religious position rather than self-refuting.
Donahue's contention that it is plainly wrong for no possible sensory evidence to make inference to theism rational.
Malpass invokes a faith-centered Christian tradition according to which belief is not settled by empirical calculation and defends religious ambiguity as non-absurd.
Case-specific comparison leaves religious ambiguity attractive, while a priori arguments for God remain available even if empirical probability cannot settle the issue.
The move consolidates the skeptical conclusion while distinguishing rejection of empirical fine-tuning inference from rejection of every possible argument for God.
Donahue's characterization of universal empirical underdetermination as a radical and highly counterintuitive implication.
Malpass rejects rhetorical appeals to irrationality, asks for detailed comparison of cases, and separates empirical ambiguity from contingency, moral, or other a priori arguments.
Theism may overcome religious ambiguity because its simplicity relative to rival hypotheses gives it greater intrinsic probability.
This frames intrinsic simplicity as the principal route by which fine-tuning can favor theism despite acknowledged religious ambiguity.
Malpass's position that the world remains religiously ambiguous and empirical probability methods cannot resolve it.
After Malpass argues that a posteriori study cannot settle the religious question, Donahue grants substantial ambiguity but challenges its inevitability by invoking theism's comparative simplicity.
A disjunction containing every specific limited alternative can have greater prior probability than the single unlimited hypothesis, reversing the proposed simplicity advantage.
The argument directly contests the claimed prior-probability advantage of unlimited divine attributes by changing how the competing hypothesis space is aggregated.
Donahue's contention that unlimited theism is simpler and therefore intrinsically more probable than its limited rivals.
Malpass recalls Paul Draper's treatment of unlimited and limited hypotheses, proposing that the summed probability of all possible limits may swamp the lone unlimited hypothesis.
Draper's appeal to modesty does not establish that limited alternatives collectively outrank theism, because coherence may outweigh modesty in determining intrinsic probability.
This response supplies the conceptual distinction between coherence and modesty on which the pro side's comparative prior-probability case substantially depends.
Malpass's argument that the disjunction of specific limited hypotheses intrinsically swamps the single unlimited-theism hypothesis.
Donahue accepts Malpass's account of Draper, explains coherence and modesty, and argues that Draper merely asserts rather than demonstrates that modesty dominates coherence.
Uncertainty about whether coherence outweighs modesty undermines confidence in the claimed asymmetry between theism and augmented naturalism.
The move identifies an unresolved comparison as the weakest link in the pro side's probability argument and uses that uncertainty to withhold its conclusion.
Donahue's claim that coherence makes theism simpler and gives it a superior specific-to-general probability ratio.
Malpass argues that Donahue's concession of uncertainty about Draper's coherence-modesty analysis reduces the earlier confidence that theism compares favorably with augmented naturalism.
Even if quasi-theistic alternatives collectively exceed theism, theism still outranks augmented naturalism because it possesses coherence while augmented naturalism has neither coherence nor modesty.
This preserves the pro side's crucial likelihood comparison without requiring resolution of whether coherence or modesty is globally the dominant intrinsic-probability factor.
Malpass's objection that unresolved weighting between coherence and modesty defeats the comparison between theism and augmented naturalism.
Donahue narrows his claim: coherence need only contribute some probability, since theism benefits from it whereas the fine-tuned naturalistic alternative is both specific and incoherent.
Naturalism's greater ontological parsimony may offset theism's advantages in coherence or modesty because theism posits natural reality plus additional supernatural entities.
The objection introduces an independent theoretical virtue that could neutralize the pro side's intrinsic-probability advantage and alter the overall comparison.
Donahue's revised argument that theism's coherence makes it intrinsically more probable than the augmented-naturalism alternative.
Malpass tentatively proposes that naturalism wins on ontological economy because theism includes everything naturalism posits and adds further supernatural commitments.
Naturalism's modest ontological-simplicity advantage is outweighed by the much larger conditional-probability advantage theism gains over augmented naturalism.
This integrates the con side's parsimony objection into the pro framework while maintaining that the fine-tuning comparison still yields a net advantage for theism.
Malpass's proposal that naturalism's fewer ontological commitments may balance or defeat theism's claimed coherence advantage.
Donahue concedes that naturalism has one kind of reality while design adds another, but argues that this limited benefit cannot plausibly match the enormous disadvantage of augmented naturalism.

Scientific universal generalizations support giving coherence greater weight than modesty, while the tiny prior share of augmented naturalism makes theism's conditional advantage swamp naturalism's parsimony benefit.
The closing consolidates the pro side's two main probability claims: coherence can dominate a disjunction of less-uniform rivals, and the decisive fine-tuning ratio overwhelms ontological simplicity.
Malpass's objections that modest alternatives collectively swamp theism and that naturalism receives a compensating advantage from ontological parsimony.

Donahue invokes uniform electron-charge hypotheses as evidence that coherence can outweigh modesty, then argues that augmented naturalism's extraordinarily small conditional probability dominates the final comparison.
Apparent fine-tuning may indicate a defect in a physical theory rather than an objective feature of the universe requiring a design explanation.
This challenges the evidential foundation of the motion by denying that theoretical fine-tuning should automatically be treated as a universe-level fact needing explanation.
Donahue's fine-tuning inference, which treats the relevant life-permitting improbability as evidence favoring a specific design hypothesis.
Malpass says physicists may regard fine-tuning as a property of theories; on that approach, severe tuning is reason to suspect the theory rather than infer an external designer.
Fine-tuning cannot strongly favor theism when divine goodness, intentions, values, and resulting choices are too uncertain to ground reliable likelihood judgments.
The argument attacks the likelihood of fine-tuning under theism itself, undercutting the Bayesian comparison even if the naturalistic alternatives are granted substantial complexity.
The pro side's use of a good God's presumed aims to assign appreciable probability to a life-permitting, fine-tuned universe under theism.
Malpass argues that one cannot simply assume a good God, know what divine goodness entails, or infer that divine reasons resemble human values enough to predict creation.
